company: University of Warwick and NHS England
headline: Nearly 700,000 women are set to be invited into an NHS trial of AI breast screening
summary: A trial called EDITH has started testing AI as a reader of NHS breast screening mammograms, beginning at Cambridge University Hospitals. Your invitation letter will tell you if your centre is taking part and how to opt out.
body: The University of Warwick says recruitment has started for EDITH, which it calls the world’s largest AI-assisted breast screening trial. Cambridge University Hospitals is the first of 30 NHS sites across the UK, and more open in the coming months. Over the next three years, nearly 700,000 women having routine NHS breast screening are expected to be invited. The National Institute for Health and Care Research is paying £10 million for it.

Today, two radiologists look at every mammogram, and fewer than 1% show signs of cancer. The trial tests whether AI can help staff spot cancers earlier by flagging areas of a scan they might miss. If the AI proves safe, many mammograms might need only one radiologist.

Your appointment stays the same. Every mammogram still goes to at least one human radiologist, and NHS staff keep all clinical decisions. The study’s information page says scans are randomly read either by two NHS experts without AI or by at least one expert using AI, and you won’t be told which.

Women aged 50 to 71 get a screening invitation every three years. If your centre joins the trial, your invitation letter explains it and how to opt out. Opt out before or at your appointment and two NHS experts read your scans without AI, and your data stays out of the results.
do_this: Read your next breast screening invitation letter for a mention of the EDITH trial.
To opt out, contact your screening centre using the details in the letter, or tell staff when you book or at your appointment.
Keep your screening appointment either way: it stays the same as before.
